Bear in mind that the modern view of pre-modern warfare - the honorable fight man against man, sword against sword - is heavily romanticized. Rather than fighting each other in large, epic battles (which were not as epic as they are made to be), pre-modern armies spent the bulk of their time weakening the enemy by devastating the countryside - pillaging and burning their way through villages, with a bit of rape thrown in for good measure.

Then there's the actual fighting. If you were lucky, you were a man-at-arms who at least was giving training, weapons, and armor by the lord he served. If you were really lucky, you'd be a knight and might even survive combat if you are critically wounded because the enemy general wants to ransom you. But chances are that you are neither, and that you are just some peasant who was forced into military service to serve as cannon fodder.

One-on-one combat hardly existed, either. Be it a disorderly horde or a well-disciplined formation, melee battle essentially was two heaps of men marching towards one another and hitting the respective other with pointy pieces of metal until one side lost moral and started running away. There was no epic personal combat. Just you trying to stab someone while also trying not to get stabbed yourself.

Long story short, the idea that pre-gunpowder warfare was something high and honorable that relied on the invidiual warrior's strength and skill is little more than a pretty image which modern history books and fantasy fiction paint of it. In many ways, pre-modern warfare actually was worse than modern one - logistics were rudimentary at best so that hunger was the permanent companion of most armies, and with medicine still in its infancy, even seemingly banal diseases could spread and incapacitate entire armies. Even if you survived a battle, seemingly minor wounds could become infected and spell a death verdict.
